description: rocketpower propone una herramienta sencilla y entretenida que combina datos de la NASA con información local sobre suelos y cultivos. Buscamos ayudar a los agricultores a explorar rotaciones que mejoren la salud del suelo, conserven agua y permitan adaptarse a un clima cambiante.
summary:
Prospector is a decision-support tool that works on any piece of land in the world. A farmer or advisor draws the field on a satellite map, and Prospector builds a 3D replica of the terrain from NASA elevation data, shows where cultivation is possible and where it is not (slope, water channels, buildings, roads, trees), and explains each answer in plain language.

For that exact place it simulates 31 annual crops day by day against 24 years of NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rainfall, and tells which crops grow without irrigation, a tentative sowing window, and how many years out of ten the harvest succeeds. It then compares the current rotation with alternatives by water use, soil loss and months of bare soil, and lays the field out in plots, asking the farmer what to do with trees, roads and field edges instead of assuming all land is usable.

The plan can be watched in 3D month by month, in a dry, a normal and a wet year taken from the real record. Every number shows its data source, and what is observed (crops actually grown nearby, measured yields) is kept separate from what is simulated. The tool supports the farmer's decision; it does not replace local agronomic advice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

1. Locate and measure. The user draws a polygon, rectangle or circle anywhere on Earth. Prospector downloads open data for that window and reports area, altitude above sea level, slope, aspect and drainage. Elevation is the average of NASADEM and Copernicus GLO-30; the difference between both is shown as the height margin of error.

2. Where can I farm? Each 10 m cell is classified from physical evidence: suitable, suitable with care (8–15 % slope), too steep, water channel and buffer, water/buildings/roads, or suitable but currently under trees or shrubs. Tapping any point in the 3D view explains why, in simple or technical language.

3. What grows here? 31 annual crops are simulated with daily NASA POWER data (MERRA-2, CERES) and GPM IMERG rainfall for 2001–2024: thermal time, FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, a soil water balance, the FAO-33 yield response to water, and frost and heat at flowering. Sowing dates and cycle length are adjusted to local practice with the GGCMI global crop calendar. Dates are tentative: the real date depends on the variety and the year. The 31 crops are annual crops and only a starting set (23 field crops plus 8 vegetable and industrial crops). Fruit trees, vines and pastures are not simulated: for 79 other crops the app reports whether they are actually grown in the area and whether the area ranks among the world's top producers, which is a market signal the farmer can weigh. Where the open map marks a parcel as vineyard or orchard, the app treats it as an existing plantation, not as woodland to clear.

4. How to rotate. For each terrain zone the current rotation is compared with alternatives: years with a good harvest out of ten, water use, soil loss (RUSLE) and months with bare soil, with the reason and the risks of each option.

5. Field layout. The tool does not assume the whole field is usable. It detects trees, moderate slopes, roads and buildings, asks the farmer what to do with each, leaves machinery headlands and buffer strips, splits the land into plots, traces the access route from the nearest road that vehicles can use, and reports what stays unplanted and why.

6. See it. The plan is shown on the 3D terrain with surrounding buildings and trees. An animation shows the access road, clearing, soil preparation and first sowing; then crops grow, ripen and leave stubble month by month.

7. Reshape it. On slopes of 8 to 30 % one button shows the hillside as bench terraces that stay connected to the rest of the field (benches about 8 m wide, access ramps from the existing roads, blended edges) with the earth to move. A separate page applies the same idea to Mars and the Moon without flattening anything: real MOLA and LOLA elevation in 3D, slopes classed with the limits real missions used, a landing pad of published size at the flattest place, the days a real robotic excavator would need to level it and whether that is worth it, and a station sited outside the reach of engine debris with a cargo access under 5 degrees. Every limit links to its source. It measures terrain shape only and says so.

WHAT IS OBSERVED AND WHAT IS SIMULATED

Simulated results (suitability, sowing date, water need) are always shown next to observed data for the same area: the share of land actually sown with each crop (CROPGRIDS) and measured yields for maize, rice, wheat and soybean (GDHY). Observed data never changes a simulated verdict; it accompanies it so the user can judge.

VALIDATION

The crop engine was tested on random points spread evenly over nine world regions, against independent data: real cropland from ESA CCI Land Cover, harvested area per crop from CROPGRIDS and the GGCMI crop calendar. On a sample of 360 points drawn after the last change to the engine and never used to adjust it: in 94 % of rainfed cropland points the engine finds at least one crop that grows without irrigation; in arid land with no cropland (under 250 mm of rain a year) it finds none (0 of 27 points); and where a given crop is really sown, the engine recognises it in 97 % of 919 cases (81 % without irrigation, 15 % only with irrigation). A second, targeted sample of 951 points taken only where each crop is grown gives 94 % recognised; the weakest crops are broad bean, pepper, pea and cabbage, and the app flags them. Weak spots: North Africa and the Middle East (76 %), maize, rice and cassava missed at 8–10 % of the places where they are sown, and sowing dates for peas and potatoes. Earlier samples exposed real errors (for example alfalfa judged on winter temperatures, or spring sowing after snowmelt treated as dry sowing); each was fixed for a physical reason and re-measured on a new sample. The scripts, the reports and the list of fixes are in the repository (docs/VALIDATION.md).

KNOWN LIMITS

Terrain resolution is 30 m. Only 31 annual crops are simulated out of the many grown worldwide; a crop missing from the list is not a crop that fails. Crop parameters are general FAO values adjusted with a 55 km crop calendar, not local varieties, so sowing and harvest dates are tentative. Roads come from OpenStreetMap/Overture and rural tracks may be missing; the user can mark the entrance by hand. No money or yield-in-tonnes projections are produced by the model. Results need review by farmers or local agricultural experts.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

Python (FastAPI, rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, pysheds), a single-page web client (MapLibre GL JS, three.js). It runs on one computer with no cloud account: 4 GB of RAM and about 4 GB of disk, and ships as a Docker image. The interface is currently in Spanish.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Most rotation tools score a single point. Prospector works on the real shape of the field: where water runs, where the slope is too steep, where the road is, what the neighbours built — and asks the farmer before deciding.

USE OF AI

The code and the written materials of this project were produced with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), directed and reviewed by the team. AI research agents collected the regional crop statistics and the Mars and Moon siting criteria, each with its source. No images, video or audio were generated with AI. The running application does not use a generative AI model.
